analysis.one_liner: Bars ex-SEC enforcers from working for firms they prosecuted for one year.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in March 2015 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it a federal crime for a former Securities and Exchange Commission employee to go to work, within a year of leaving, for a company or individual the SEC had prosecuted for an enforcement action the employee personally worked on. Before taking such a job, the former employee would have needed an ethics opinion from the SEC confirming there was no appearance of impropriety. The goal was to close part of the "revolving door" between the SEC and the firms it polices.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary investors and the public, who rely on SEC enforcement being free of insider influence. It would also have protected the integrity of ongoing SEC cases and the staff who bring them, and levelled the playing field for companies that compete against firms with ex-SEC hires on staff.

how_it_helps.text: A former SEC employee who, within one year of leaving, worked for a company or individual the SEC had prosecuted — in a matter the employee personally participated in during the previous 18 months — would face the same federal criminal penalties as for bribery and conflicts-of-interest offenses.

Former SEC staff would have to obtain an SEC ethics opinion before taking such a job, and the SEC could only permit it by finding no appearance of impropriety, no material advantage to the employer, and no damage to the integrity of the ongoing enforcement action.
The ban would cover not just employment but also volunteering, lobbying, and consulting for the former target of an enforcement action, closing common side-door routes.

analysis.who_pays: Former SEC employees, who would face a one-year restriction on working for — or consulting for or lobbying on behalf of — companies they had helped prosecute, and the financial firms that hire ex-SEC enforcers for their insider knowledge. The SEC would also bear the cost of issuing ethics opinions and reporting to Congress on how the rule affected its ability to recruit and keep staff.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ex-SEC staff and financial firms hiring them

drawbacks.text: The restriction applies only to one year of employment and only to matters the employee worked on in the prior 18 months, so much of the revolving door — including hiring SEC alumni with general expertise or knowledge of the agency's priorities — would remain entirely lawful.

The bill itself directed the SEC Chairman to report to Congress on how the restriction affected recruitment and retention of employees, an acknowledgment that it could make it harder for the agency to hire and keep experienced enforcers.

It restricts the employment choices of former federal workers, including non-lobbying consulting work, and applies criminal penalties to individuals rather than only to the firms that profit from insider knowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — protecting securities enforcement from former enforcers cashing in on the cases they worked — is real but modest in scope: the rule covers only a one-year window and only the specific matters an employee participated in. The main costs fall on a small group (recent ex-SEC staff) and on firms' ability to hire them, and the bill's own recruitment-and-retention report requirement shows supporters recognized a real risk of making SEC careers less attractive. On balance a reasonable, if narrow, ethics safeguard.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Stephen Lynch introduced the bill on March 19, 2015, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
That was the bill's only action: no subcommittee or full committee markup, no floor vote, and no Senate action ever followed before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
The bill drew only one cosponsor in two years.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial firms that hire former SEC enforcers — and the former employees themselves — are better off because the bill died; nothing ever restricted that hiring pipeline.

for.name: Rep. Stephen F. Lynch
for.role: Sponsor; member of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the SEC Revolving Door Restriction Act and referred it to the Financial Services Committee.

against.name: Jeb Hensarling
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: The committee under his chairmanship never scheduled the bill for a markup or a vote; referral was its only action in two years.

sides.party_line_note: Only two members ever acted on the bill, both Democrats (the sponsor and one cosponsor); the Republican-led Financial Services Committee took no action, so no party-line roll-call ever occurred.

industries.note: The bill would have cut off a one-year window in which firms could hire SEC enforcers who had just worked cases against them, or brought them on as consultants or lobbyists. Firms value these hires for insider knowledge of enforcement strategy; the bill treated that advantage as a conflict of interest.

Recent ex-SEC employees who worked on an enforcement matter would have faced criminal exposure for taking related private-sector work within a year. Most would remain free to leave for unrelated work in the industry.
